a: Prune is a free, open-source structural linter for TypeScript and JavaScript. It reads your whole module graph to find what coding agents tend to leave behind: dead exports, unreachable files, duplicate types, god files, import cycles and near-duplicate functions. It then turns those findings into tasks an agent can work through and verify.

q: Do I need to configure anything?
a: Usually not. Ask your coding agent to follow https://prunecode.ai/setup and it handles the install, the baseline, the pre-commit hook and the MCP connection, using whatever your repo already has. Defaults work without a .prunerc. You only touch config to exclude generated code or tune thresholds.
Yes. Prune is MIT licensed and free for any use, including commercial. There is no account, no license key and no paid tier.

q: Does my code leave my machine?
a: No. Prune is a single binary that parses, indexes and analyzes your code locally. A scan makes no network calls. The optional semantic matching uses a small embedding model that runs locally and is only downloaded when you enable it.

q: Which languages and frameworks does Prune support?
a: TypeScript and JavaScript (.ts, .tsx, .js, .jsx, .mts, .mjs, .cts, .cjs). Entry points are discovered from package.json, tool configs, scripts and shebang files, and there are built-in adapters for Next.js routes and Convex functions.

q: How is Prune different from ESLint or an unused-exports tool?
a: ESLint and tsc check code file by file. Unused-export tools report what nothing imports. Prune classifies every export by how far it is from used (used, test_only, same_file_only, unused, unreachable). It also finds duplicate shapes, god files and import cycles, and it hands each finding to your agent as a task with a verify command.

q: How do I use Prune with Claude Code, Cursor or another agent?
a: Tell your agent: "Set up Prune in this repo by following https://prunecode.ai/setup." The setup page is written for agents. It installs Prune with your package manager, adds the pre-commit check, and connects the MCP server (for Claude Code: `claude mcp add prune -- npx prune mcp`). After that, the agent can call tasks, verify, who_uses, safe_to_delete and rename_impact on its own.

q: Will Prune block commits because of existing debt?
a: Not if you record a baseline. Run `prune baseline` once and commit .prune-baseline.json. After that, `prune check` in pre-commit and `prune scan --baseline --ci` fail only on findings that are new.

Only the mechanical ones: dropping export from symbols that only their own file uses, and deleting unreachable files. `prune fix --apply --check "<your typecheck>"` applies each fix, runs your check, and reverts the fix if the check fails. Everything else becomes a task for you or your agent.
